Cosine function. One of the fundamental trigonometric functions, mapping angles to the ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse in a right triangle. Defined for all real numbers and taking values between minus one and one, the cosine function is periodic with period two pi and appears ubiquitously in physics, engineering, and harmonic analysis.

The cosine of an angle in a right triangle is the length of the adjacent side divided by the length of the hypotenuse. This geometric definition extends to all angles via the unit circle. As a periodic function, cosine of theta plus two pi equals cosine of theta. Its graph oscillates smoothly between minus one and one with a wavelike pattern, making it ideal for modeling cyclic phenomena.

The cosine function is even: cosine of negative theta equals cosine of theta, reflecting symmetry about the vertical axis. This symmetry simplifies many calculations and appears throughout mathematics. Via Euler's formula, cosine is the real part of the complex exponential: cosine of theta equals the real part of e to the i theta, which equals e to the i theta plus e to the negative i theta all divided by two. This bridges trigonometry and complex analysis.

Fourier analysis decomposes periodic signals into sums of cosines and sines, fundamental to signal processing, audio compression, image processing, and quantum mechanics. The derivative of cosine is negative sine: the derivative of cosine with respect to x is negative sine of x. This makes cosine and sine deeply intertwined through calculus. Repeatedly differentiating cycles between them.

Cosine appears in the law of cosines, relating side lengths in triangles, in dot products of vectors, and in countless physics applications from wave mechanics to orbital mechanics. The cosine approximation—cosine of x approximately equals one minus x squared over two for small x—enables linear stability analysis and perturbation theory across science and engineering, illustrating why the function's structure matters for applications.
